Purpose and scope This runbook gives on-call engineers a consistent way to diagnose and resolve production incidents across the eight core Contoso services: payment-gateway, auth-service, order-api, inventory-service, notification-service, search-service, reporting-engine and user-profile-api. It covers the ten most frequent error codes seen in the incident log over the last two quarters. Each error code has a symptom description, likely causes, a diagnostic checklist, a fix, and a prevention note. 2. How to use this runbook Start from the error code in the alert or log line. Confirm the symptom matches, work through the diagnostic checklist in order, and apply the fix only after the cause is confirmed. If two consecutive diagnostic steps produce no signal, escalate according to the severity matrix in Section 3. Always record the root cause category in the incident ticket; reporting depends on it. 3. Golden rules 1) Check recent deployments first: roughly one in four incidents in the log is deploy related, and a rollback is almost always faster than a forward fix. 2) Never restart a stateful component before capturing logs and a heap or thread dump. 3) Communicate early: post in the incident channel within five minutes of acknowledging any Sev1 or Sev2. 4) Change one thing at a time and note the time of each change in the ticket. If the primary on-call has not acknowledged an alert within the ack target, the page automatically escalates to the secondary on-call and then to the team lead. 7. Standard first five minutes 1. Acknowledge the alert and open an incident ticket (INC-xxxx). 2. Identify the error code and service from the alert payload. 3. Check the deploy dashboard: was anything released in the last 2 hours? 4. Check dependency health: status page for each critical dependency. 5. Post the first update in #incidents with service, code, severity, owner. 8. Useful commands kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=<service> -o wide kubectl logs deploy/<service> -n prod --since=30m | grep -i error kubectl describe pod <pod> -n prod | grep -A5 "Last State" kubectl rollout undo deploy/<service> -n prod Rollback note: kubectl rollout undo reverts to the previous ReplicaSet. Database migrations are not reverted automatically; check the migration log before rolling back a release that includes a schema change. Contoso Platform Engineering | Troubleshooting Runbook v3.2 | Internal - Synthetic demo data Page 3 Authentication and Rate Limiting Errors ERR-401 - Expired or invalid authentication token Symptom: Clients receive HTTP 401 with body {"error":"token_expired"}; spikes often follow a deployment of auth-service or a change to token lifetime configuration. user-profile-api and payment-gateway are the most affected consumers. Likely causes: (a) access token TTL shortened in config; (b) clock skew above 30 seconds between services; (c) signing key rotated but the JWKS cache in the consumer was not refreshed; (d) refresh-token flow failing silently in the client SDK. Diagnostics: 1. Compare the exp and iat claims of a failing token. 2. Check NTP sync on the affected nodes (chronyc tracking). 3. Confirm the JWKS endpoint returns the newest key id (kid). 4. Look for a recent change to AUTH_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS. Fix: Restore the previous TTL (default 900 seconds), force a JWKS refresh by restarting the consumer pods one at a time, and fix NTP drift if present. Ask client teams to enable proactive refresh 60 seconds before expiry. Prevention: Alert when 401 rate exceeds 2% for five minutes; require a canary check on every key rotation. ERR-429 - Rate limit exceeded Symptom: HTTP 429 responses with a Retry-After header. Most common on notification-service (burst campaigns) and auth-service (login storms). Throttling is enforced at the API gateway using a token-bucket policy per API key. Likely causes: A batch job calling without backoff; a retry storm after an upstream timeout; a misconfigured quota after a plan change; a bot or credential-stuffing attack on login endpoints. Diagnostics: 1.

or credential-stuffing attack on login endpoints. Diagnostics: 1. Identify the top API keys by request volume in the gateway dashboard. 2. Check whether 429s began right after a 5xx burst (retry storm). 3. Inspect the user agent and IP distribution for attack patterns. Fix: Ask the offending client to apply exponential backoff with jitter (base 200 ms, cap 30 s). Temporarily raise the quota for legitimate batch jobs. For attacks, enable the WAF rate rule and block the offending ranges. Prevention: Publish client retry guidance; schedule batch jobs outside peak hours; set per-key burst limits lower than sustained limits. Contoso Platform Engineering | Troubleshooting Runbook v3.2 | Internal - Synthetic demo data Page 4 Application and Gateway Errors ERR-500 - Unhandled exception Symptom: HTTP 500 with a stack trace in the service logs. In the incident log this code has the highest share of deploy-related incidents (about 45%). order-api, inventory-service and user-profile-api are the main sources. Likely causes: Null or missing field in a new payload shape; an unhandled promise rejection or exception in a new code path; a feature flag enabled before its dependent migration ran; a library upgrade that changed default behaviour. Diagnostics: 1. Find the first occurrence timestamp and match it to a deploy. 2. Group stack traces by top frame to find the single failing line. 3. Reproduce with the failing request from the access log in staging. kubectl logs deploy/order-api -n prod --since=1h | grep -A8 "Traceback" Fix: Roll back the release. Then add a guard or default for the failing field, add a regression test that reproduces the payload, and redeploy through the canary pipeline. Prevention: Contract tests for every producer/consumer pair; mandatory canary at 5% traffic for 15 minutes. ERR-503 - Downstream dependency unavailable Symptom: HTTP 503 with 'upstream connect error' or circuit breaker open messages. Typical for payment-gateway (bank API), notification-service (email/SMS vendor) and search-service (catalog indexer). Diagnostics: 1. Check the vendor status page. 2. Test connectivity from a debug pod (curl with timing). 3. Confirm circuit breaker state and failure threshold. 4. Look for DNS resolution failures in the sidecar logs. Fix: Fail over to the secondary provider where one exists, enable degraded mode (queue and retry later), and communicate expected recovery time to stakeholders. Do not repeatedly restart healthy pods. ERR-504 - Gateway timeout Symptom: HTTP 504 after 30 seconds; p95 latency above 3,000 ms. The week of 10 August 2026 saw a cluster of ERR-504 incidents on payment-gateway, traced to slow queries on the payments-db after an index was dropped during a migration. Likely causes: Slow database queries; thread pool saturation; a slow downstream call without a timeout; an under-provisioned pod count after a traffic increase. Diagnostics: 1.

pod count after a traffic increase. Diagnostics: 1. Check p95 latency per endpoint. 2. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on the slowest query (see Section 5 database errors). 3. Check HTTP client timeouts: every outbound call must have an explicit timeout of 5 seconds or less. 4. Check HPA status. Fix: Restore any missing index, set explicit client timeouts, scale out replicas, and enable request hedging for idempotent reads. Contoso Platform Engineering | Troubleshooting Runbook v3.2 | Internal - Synthetic demo data Page 5 Database Errors DB-1205 - Lock wait timeout exceeded Symptom: Queries fail with 'Lock wait timeout exceeded; try restarting transaction'. Latency climbs to 2 seconds or more and then writes begin to fail. Seen on payment-gateway, inventory-service and order-api. Likely causes: Long-running transactions holding row locks; missing index causing table-level scans during updates; batch updates that lock too many rows; inconsistent lock ordering across code paths causing deadlock-like waits. Diagnostics: -- PostgreSQL: find blockers and blocked sessions SELECT blocked.pid AS blocked_pid, blocked.query AS blocked_query, blocking.pid AS blocking_pid, blocking.query AS blocking_query, now() - blocking.xact_start AS blocking_duration FROM pg_stat_activity blocked JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) ORDER BY blocking_duration DESC; Fix: Cancel the blocking session if it is an idle-in-transaction connection (SELECT pg_cancel_backend(pid)). Break batch updates into chunks of 500 rows. Add the missing index and standardise lock ordering. Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout to 60 seconds. Prevention: Keep transactions short; never call external services inside a transaction; review every migration for lock impact. DB-POOL - Connection pool exhausted Symptom: Errors such as 'timeout waiting for connection from pool' or 'remaining connection slots are reserved'. The service looks healthy but all requests that touch the database hang for the pool wait time (default 30 seconds). order-api and user-profile-api are the most frequent offenders. Likely causes: Connection leak (a code path acquires but never releases); pool size too small after a replica count increase; slow queries holding connections longer than expected; a deployment that doubled the number of pods and exceeded the database max_connections. Diagnostics: 1. Compare active vs idle connections: SELECT state, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY state. 2. Check pool metrics (active, idle, pending). 3. Search recent changes for code that opens a connection outside a context manager or try/finally. 4. Compare max_connections to pods multiplied by pool size. Fix: Restart the leaking pods one at a time to release connections, then patch the leak (use context managers). Right-size the pool: pool_size x replicas must be less than 80% of max_connections. Consider PgBouncer in transaction mode for services with many replicas. Prevention: Alert when pool utilisation exceeds 85% for five minutes; add a leak-detection threshold of 20 seconds in non-production.

Contoso Platform Engineering | Troubleshooting Runbook v3.2 | Internal - Synthetic demo data Page 6 Infrastructure Errors MEM-OOM - Container OOMKilled Symptom: Pods restart repeatedly; kubectl describe shows 'Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137'. Common on search-service (large result sets) and reporting-engine (big in-memory aggregations). Likely causes: Memory limit set below real working set; unbounded caches or result sets; memory leak introduced by a release; JVM heap configured larger than the container limit; a report requested over an unusually large date range. Diagnostics: 1. Check memory graph for a saw-tooth pattern (leak) versus a step (large request). 2. Confirm the limit: kubectl get pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[*].resources}'. 3. Capture a heap dump before the next restart. 4. Identify the request that precedes each kill. Fix: Raise the limit by 25 to 50 percent as a stop-gap, paginate or stream large results, add max-range validation on report requests, and set JVM -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70. Prevention: Load test with production-sized datasets; alert at 85% memory utilisation. DISK-FULL - Disk usage above 95% Symptom: Write failures, 'No space left on device', failed log rotation, search index shards moving to read-only (flood stage watermark on OpenSearch). Affects inventory-service, search-service and reporting-engine. Diagnostics: 1. df -h and du -sh /var/log/* to find the largest directories. 2. Check for orphaned temp files from failed ETL runs. 3. For OpenSearch, check shard sizes and the read-only block: GET _cluster/settings and GET _all/_settings?filter_path=*.settings.index.blocks. Fix: Delete rotated logs older than seven days and orphaned temp files. Expand the volume. For OpenSearch, free space then clear the read-only block (PUT _all/_settings with index.blocks.read_only_allow_delete set to null). Prevention: Enforce log retention of seven days; alert at 80% disk usage; add lifecycle policies to indices. CERT-EXP - TLS certificate expired Symptom: Clients fail with 'certificate has expired' or 'SSL handshake failed'. Often hits auth-service because it terminates TLS for many internal clients. Latency is low because connections fail immediately. Diagnostics: echo | openssl s_client -connect auth.contoso.internal:443 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -dates kubectl get certificate -A | grep -v True Fix: Renew the certificate through cert-manager (kubectl cert-manager renew ), reload the ingress controller, and verify the full chain. If the ACME challenge fails, check DNS-01 credentials. Prevention: Alert 30, 14 and 7 days before expiry; never rely on a manual renewal calendar. Post-incident checklist 1. Incident ticket has root cause category, error code, resolution time and deploy-related flag. 2. Timeline reconstructed from alerts, deploys and chat. 3. A blameless review is scheduled within five business days for every Sev1 and Sev2. 4. At least one preventive action item is created, with an owner and a due date. 5. Runbook updated if a diagnostic step was missing or wrong. C. Metrics we track Mean time to acknowledge (MTTA), mean time to resolve (MTTR) per severity, percentage of incidents that are deploy related, repeat-incident rate per error code, and number of incidents detected by customers before monitoring. Targets for the current quarter: MTTR for Sev2 below 120 minutes; deploy-related incidents below 20 percent; zero repeat Sev1 incidents with the same root cause. D.
